newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leader sworn in as head of state.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leader sworn in as head of state.

text.p: Sierra Leone's military leader, Johnny Paul Koroma, was sworn in as head of state on Tuesday and pledged to restore peace and eventually democracy to the war-weary West African nation.

Koroma, who heads an Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC) formed after junior officers who toppled elected civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah on May 25, was sworn in by Chief Justice Samuel Beccles Davies at a low-key ceremony.

"We are committed to bringing this country to a lasting peace and then eventually returning the country to a democratically elected government," he said after the ceremony at military headquarters in the capital.
"We will form a very broad-based government incorporating every sector of the community. We will make sure that every tribe is represented," he added.

Koroma said that both the rebel Revolutionary United Front, which took up arms in 1991 and has rallied to the coup, and Kamajor traditional hunters who have kept their distance from the coup leaders and have clashed with the army, would be represented.
Kamajor leaders, whose forces formed a civil militia under Kabbah, have said they will not join a broad-based government and want to stay out of politics.
About 100 people attended the ceremony at military headquarters in the capital Freetown. They included senior military officers, religious leaders, lawyers and businessmen.
Koroma urged the outside world "to see" the impoverished yet mineral-rich country's problems "and make a speedy move to get the peace process on the move again".
Civilian politicians and Sierra Leone's West African neighbours insist that Kabbah be reinstated, something the coup leaders have rejected.
The coup leaders accuse Kabbah of humiliating the army, inciting tribalism and blocking peace with the rebels.

Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital Freetown in a show of force on June 2 and dissident soldiers and rebels attacked Nigerian soldiers who were there under a defence accord. The United States, France, Lebanon and other nations evacuated their own and other foreign nationals.
A widely anticipated Nigerian attack has not materialised.
